criteria.ref: 1.1 — Understanding of the terms of reference (5 points)
criteria.whatScoresWell: Proving understanding rather than restating the background. Four things earn the mark: (a) naming the boundary CI itself sets — this assignment designs the DELIVERY VEHICLE for brands, not the brands or identities themselves, which subsequent assignments will implement; (b) adopting CI's own framing of a spectrum from a grant-funded technical-assistance retainer to a commercially run platform, and showing the spectrum has more than two points on it; (c) showing the scale problem — 15 emerging areas today inside a 162-KPA, US$1.2bn-a-year partnership, so a model built for 15 must stretch toward 162; (d) treating the nine mandatory elaboration headings (offer, results, stakeholders, information and cash flows, funding needs over time, governance, funders, case studies, six-way pros and cons) and the seven design aims as the TEMPLATE for the work, not a checklist bolted on at the end. Naming Africa's Eden and Boundless Southern Africa with one specific, non-obvious fact about each (Africa's Eden is pay-to-play and private-sector-led across eight countries; Boundless has been publicly hosted since 2007 and publishes no recognition or booking outcomes) converts assertion into evidence. Quoting CI's own test — fill gaps rather than duplicate efforts — and answering it.
criteria.whatLosesPoints: Paraphrasing the RFP background back at the evaluator. Offering to create park brands, logos or identities, which is explicitly out of scope and reads as not having read the ToR. Generic destination-marketing language. Treating financial sustainability as one bullet among many when the ToR puts it first and repeats it three times. Silence on the hard constraints (12 weeks, desk-based, no travel, US$40,000) as shapers of the method. Listing the nine headings without showing them structuring anything.
criteria.whereInResponse: Page 1 of the 5-page body, under a heading that mirrors the criterion wording ('Our understanding of the assignment and expected outcomes'), plus a boxed 'What we already know' panel referencing Annex C (the 31-benchmark scan). Do not scatter this across the document — the evaluator scores it from one place.
criteria.eyPositionToday: strong — this is fully writable from the inputs in hand, and the benchmark draft lets EY demonstrate understanding at a depth no competitor can match on a blank page. Highest-confidence 5 points in the document.

criteria.ref: 1.2 — Relevant experience to undertake the assignment, 5-10 years (20 points)
criteria.whatScoresWell: This is the largest single criterion in the whole scoring table — 20 of 70 technical points, more than understanding, methodology and geography combined. It is scored against the eight skills CI lists in Section 3 (offeror requirements): brand development and destination branding; business planning, business models and financial modelling; global tourism and brand development/management exposure; proven ability to work with the private sector and secure investment or funding; business cases and pitching; stakeholder management and partnerships; Africa region and tourism landscape; protected areas and conservation. What scores is a table of six to eight named engagements spanning a 5-10 year track record, each row carrying client, country, dates, the EY legal entity that delivered it, EY's role, engagement magnitude, and a tick against which of the eight skills it proves — with full coverage of all eight, above all the two that most bidders cannot show: protected areas/conservation, and securing private investment or funding. Continuity over 5-10 years beats one impressive recent job. If a skill genuinely is not in EY SA's book, a named consortium or subcontract partner closes it credibly; the RFP expressly permits partnership or consortium.
criteria.whatLosesPoints: Firm-wide boilerplate ('EY is a global leader in...') with no engagement-level evidence — this is the single most common way 20 points becomes 8. Undated credentials. Unnamed clients ('a major African conservation body'). Padding the list with adjacent-sector work (financial services, payments, public sector digital) that does not map to any of the eight skills. Leaving conservation/protected-area experience unproven and hoping the methodology carries it. Claiming reach the annex dossier does not evidence, which invites the evaluator to discount the whole table.
criteria.whereInResponse: Page 3 of the body, as a scoreable table that stands on its own without the annex — the evaluator must be able to award the 20 points without turning a page. Annex B carries the full dossier with the 'detailed reference list indicating the scope and magnitude of similar assignments' that Part 1 separately requires. Note the three different time windows in play: 5-10 years here, 'last three years' at 2.2, and 'past five (5) years' in the Part 1 submission requirement — build one dated table that satisfies all three rather than three lists.
criteria.eyPositionToday: blocked on missing input. Nothing in the inputs contains a single EY credential, client name, engagement date or engagement value. EY can build the table structure and the skill-coverage map today; the content is entirely dependent on [[TO CONFIRM: six to eight EY engagements from the last 5-10 years, each with client name, country, start and end dates, delivering EY legal entity, EY's role, fee band or engagement magnitude, and which of the eight RFP skill areas it evidences — supplied by Michael Harris from the EY SA Business Consulting credentials library, with client naming clearance obtained for each]]. This is the critical path for the whole bid.

criteria.ref: 2.1 — Methodology and delivery approach within the provided timelines (5 points)
criteria.whatScoresWell: A plan that visibly lands the four deliverables on the dates CI names — inception week 2, situational analysis and best practice draft week 5, models draft plus presentation week 10, final report week 12 — with a week-by-week bar chart and CI review turnarounds stated as assumptions. What lifts this above a compliant plan is showing that weeks 1-5 are not spent building a long-list, because the long-list already exists: 31 benchmarks across seven archetypes, 13 already triaged into eight deep-dive case studies and five light-touch checks. That converts the tightest part of the schedule into a de-risked head start. Also scoring: the nine CI headings applied as a fixed template to every model so comparison is like-for-like; the design-aims matrix used as the explicit, pre-agreed frame for recommending the preferred model rather than a post-hoc justification; a named interview list (Boundless secretariat, Africa's Eden Tourism, KAZA, NRT, NACSO, MMWCA, The Long Run, Preferred Hotel Group and SLH on hosting terms) instead of 'we will engage stakeholders'; an honest statement that eight case studies plus five checks is what US$40,000 over 12 weeks desk-based can actually carry; and a named mitigation for the known evidence gaps — no published member fees from the commercial collectives, no published recognition or booking outcomes from Boundless or KAZA.
criteria.whatLosesPoints: Generic consulting phases (mobilise / analyse / synthesise) with no dates. Promising primary research volume the budget cannot fund — the evaluator reads this alongside the cost proposal and a plan that does not reconcile to the fee damages both scores. Silence on the weeks 10-12 loop, when comments from CI and multiple stakeholder groups must be incorporated. Ignoring the footnote that presentations may be needed to different stakeholder groups. No risk register.
criteria.whereInResponse: Page 2 of the body in full, with the Gantt compressed into the page. Annex E carries the week-by-week detail, the RACI and the interview schedule.
criteria.eyPositionToday: strong — fully writable today, and Section 7 of EY's own benchmark draft already sets out the four method choices this section needs. Second-highest-confidence block after 1.1.

criteria.ref: 2.2 — Relevant services provided in the last three years, with samples of work delivered (15 points)
criteria.whatScoresWell: The criterion has two halves and both must be satisfied: recent services (2023-2026 only) AND attached samples of the actual work product. Three to five engagements, each paired with a named, attachable, client-cleared sample, each sample resembling something CI is actually buying — a situational analysis, a comparative options assessment, a financial sustainability model, a board-level recommendation pack, a drafted terms of reference. A short table stating for each sample what it is, when it was delivered, for whom, what it achieved, and which annex page holds it. Samples that show method (sourced evidence, comparative scoring, explicit assumptions) score better than glossy outputs.
criteria.whatLosesPoints: Listing services without samples — the criterion says 'with samples of work delivered', so a list alone forfeits a large share of 15 points. Reaching back beyond three years to pad the list; older work belongs at 1.2. Unredacted confidential client material, or samples without consent. Above all, submitting the SA banking payments POV deck that sits in the inputs: it is marked 'Draft — not for distribution', it is financial services rather than tourism, conservation or destination branding, and it would simultaneously breach a distribution restriction and score near zero on relevance. It is not a usable credential for this bid.
criteria.whereInResponse: Page 3 lower block, immediately beneath the 1.2 experience table so the evaluator scores 35 points from one page. Samples themselves in Annex B. The 31-benchmark scan belongs in Annex C and must be labelled as an EY bid-stage working paper prepared for this opportunity — it is genuine EY work product and it is powerful evidence of capability, but it is not a service delivered to a client in the last three years and presenting it as one would be a misrepresentation the evaluator can catch.
criteria.eyPositionToday: blocked on missing input. No EY samples, recent engagements or client consents are in the inputs, and the one attachable artefact in the pack is unusable. Placeholder required: [[TO CONFIRM: three to five EY engagements completed between 2023 and 2026 in destination branding, tourism, conservation finance or business-model design, each with a redacted sample deliverable cleared for external distribution, the client's written consent to name them, and a one-line outcome statement — supplied by Michael Harris with EY SA quality and independence clearance for each sample]].

criteria.whatScoresWell: The criterion has a reach half and a familiarity half; both must be answered. Reach: named EY offices and delivery presence across Southern, Eastern and Western Africa, since CI's 15 priority areas span all three; the working languages covered, which matters concretely for Angola, Mozambique and Madagascar (Portuguese and French) and for any West African area; and prior delivery in specific named countries. Familiarity: demonstrated, not asserted — SADC's TFCA architecture and the 12 formally recognised TFCAs behind Boundless; KAZA's five states, its Rivers of Life brand hub and the UniVisa; Namibia's 86 communal conservancies, NACSO and the shared Event Book data spine; Kenya's 2013 wildlife act, MMWCA's 24 conservancies and the lease-fee economics; the SANParks Wild Card pooling 80+ parks across five agencies; Fair Trade Tourism's mutual recognition across eight countries. Also scoring: naming how the model must sit with national tourism boards rather than beside them, and acknowledging that CI's list of 15 priority areas is not yet disclosed, with a method that handles its arrival at inception.
criteria.whatLosesPoints: A world map of EY's global footprint with no Africa specificity. Treating 'Africa' as a single market. Claiming country presence that cannot be evidenced. Omitting the lusophone and francophone dimension. Asserting familiarity in adjectives ('deep experience across the continent') where evidence was available.
criteria.whereInResponse: Page 4, upper block, laid out as two columns headed Reach and Familiarity so the evaluator can see both halves answered. Country and office detail can spill to an annex, but the scoreable summary must be on page 4.
criteria.eyPositionToday: partial. The familiarity half is the strongest evidenced claim EY can make today and can be written entirely from the benchmark draft without inventing anything. The reach half is blocked: [[TO CONFIRM: EY office locations and delivery presence in Southern, Eastern and Western African countries relevant to CI's priority areas, working languages available to this engagement including Portuguese and French, and any prior EY delivery in those named countries — supplied by Michael Harris from EY Africa]]. Realistically 6-7 of 10 is defensible on familiarity alone; the last 3-4 needs the office and language confirmation.

criteria.ref: 3.1 — Qualifications and competence of key staff (15 points)
criteria.whatScoresWell: A small, affordable, named team with visible accountability. Michael Harris, Partner, EY Business Consulting South Africa, named as engagement partner with a stated personal time commitment — not a figurehead. Four to six roles, each row carrying name, role, qualification, years of relevant experience, which of CI's eight skill areas the person covers, languages, and DAYS ALLOCATED ON THIS ASSIGNMENT. The days must reconcile exactly with the work plan on page 2 and with the day counts in the cost proposal; evaluators cross-check and a mismatch damages three scores at once. Visible destination-branding and protected-area/conservation expertise somewhere in the team, by consortium member or named associate if it is not in-house — its absence is the most likely reason this criterion underscores. CVs in Annex A in a consistent one-page format: education, years, three most relevant assignments, languages.
criteria.whatLosesPoints: A senior partner fronting the team with three days of input while unnamed staff deliver. Roles without day allocations. 'EY specialists will be assigned as required.' CVs of inconsistent length and format, or multi-page partner biographies. A team so large it cannot be afforded inside US$40,000, or so thin it cannot credibly deliver eight case studies, five checks and four deliverables in 12 weeks. No conservation or branding specialist anywhere on the list.
criteria.whereInResponse: Page 4, lower block — this is Part 2 of the technical proposal (Management, Key Personnel and Staffing Plan), and under the disciplined 5-page reading it must be summarised inside the body with CVs in Annex A. A staffing table plus a three-line statement of how the team is managed and who CI's single point of contact is.
criteria.eyPositionToday: blocked on missing input. Michael Harris's name and role are the only staffing facts available, and they come from the brief, not from the RFP inputs. Everything else requires [[TO CONFIRM: for each proposed team member — full name, role on this assignment, professional qualification, years of relevant experience, languages, three most relevant prior assignments, days allocated to this engagement, and a one-page CV in a common format; plus confirmation of whether a destination-branding or protected-area specialist is available in-house or must be brought in by consortium or subcontract — supplied by Michael Harris, with each named individual's availability confirmed for the 12-week window]].

criteria.ref: B — Financial proposal: clarity, relevance, reality to market value / value for money (30 points)
criteria.whatScoresWell: First and most important: this is only read if the technical proposal qualifies. The RFP states that only the financial proposals of bidders who qualify technically will be reviewed — so 30 points are gated behind technical compliance and technical quality. Within the cost PDF, what scores: a budget table with unit price, quantity and total for every line, because the RFP demands unit prices and quantities explicitly; day rates by grade with days per deliverable that reconcile line-for-line with the staffing table and the work plan; a budget narrative explaining the basis of estimate for EVERY line item, as the RFP requires; a payment schedule tied to the four deliverables with inception at or below 10% (for example 10 / 25 / 35 / 30); an explicit all-inclusive statement covering profit, fees and taxes; a tax line with a statement on minimising taxes and passing back any refunds; no travel or expense lines, because the assignment is desk-based; all figures in USD; a total that sits inside US$40,000 with visible headroom; and a short value-for-money paragraph tying the price to the head start — CI is not paying for the five weeks of benchmark scanning EY has already done.
criteria.whatLosesPoints: A lump sum with no line items — this alone can halve the 30. Day counts that contradict the technical proposal. Exceeding US$40,000, or landing on exactly US$40,000 with no contingency, which reads as reverse-engineered. More than 10% on the inception report, which is an explicit breach. Any currency other than USD. Missing tax treatment. Travel, per diem or expense lines in a no-travel assignment. A price so low it fails the 'reality to market value' test and signals either junior-only delivery or a scope the bidder does not intend to honour. Conversely, an EY standard rate card applied unadjusted will not fit US$40,000 for a 12-week, four-deliverable assignment — the fee approval, not the arithmetic, is the real obstacle.
criteria.whereInResponse: The separate Cost Proposal PDF only: budget table, budget narrative, deliverable-linked payment schedule, tax statement, assumptions. No price, rate, day rate or total appears anywhere in the technical PDF — cost leakage into a technical file that is evaluated first is a standard disqualification risk and there is no upside to it. The technical proposal expresses effort in days only.
criteria.eyPositionToday: partial. The entire structure is buildable today — line-item shape, the four-deliverable payment schedule at 10/25/35/30, the narrative headings, the USD and tax statements, the no-travel position, and the value-for-money argument. What is blocked: [[TO CONFIRM: EY day rates by grade approved for this bid, the contracting EY legal entity and its registration details, the applicable VAT/withholding tax position on a USD contract with Conservation International and whether any refund is available, and partner-level approval of the total fee against the US$40,000 all-inclusive ceiling — supplied by Michael Harris with EY SA finance and pricing]]. Also blocked: the RFP text ends mid-sentence in 'Level of Effort and Cost of Services' after stating the US$40,000 maximum and 'largely desk-based with virtual', so any level-of-effort ceiling, required staff mix or rate constraint CI may have set is unknown.

winThemes: We have already started, and here is the proof. EY holds a 31-benchmark scan across seven archetypes, already triaged into eight deep-dive case studies and five light-touch checks, with the named CI references — Africa's Eden and Boundless Southern Africa — already profiled. CI's week 1 begins at the deep-dive, not the long-list. In a 12-week, US$40,000, desk-based assignment this is the difference between a plan that is plausible and one that is already de-risked; it is the single strongest differentiator available and it should be visible on page 1, page 2 and in Annex C.

Fill the gap, do not duplicate the effort — CI's own test, answered with evidence. The aggregation layer already exists in much of CI's target geography (NACSO across 86 Namibian conservancies, NRT across 43, MMWCA across 24 with CI's own Maasai Mara Rescue Fund history), and Africa's marquee lodges are already curated by Beyond Green, National Geographic Unique Lodges and Relais & Châteaux. The brand gap is the emerging areas' back office. That finding shapes every model EY proposes and proves EY read the ToR rather than the background.

Financial sustainability is designed in, not appended. Every model carries a named payer, a mapped information and cash flow, and a funding-need curve over time, because the benchmark evidence is unambiguous: brands endure when members or visitors pay for what they deliver, and the donor-seeded networks in the set contracted or were restructured — the EUROPARC Charter from 164 areas to 91, Alpine Pearls from about 24 villages to 18, EDEN redesigned after evaluation, Fair Trade Tourism folded into an industry partnership.

Credible across borders because it is built on standards with consequences and national boards as partners, not rivals. Blue Flag scales through national operators with annual re-award; Geoparks issue yellow and red cards; Slovenia Green runs a bronze-to-platinum pathway that reconciles inclusion with credibility for sites of uneven capacity. And Tourism Australia, Slovenia and KAZA all show the model giving the national brand product and proof rather than a competing identity. These two rules make a model survivable across CI's Southern, Eastern and Western African geographies.

Delivery certainty: four deliverables on the dates named, a named partner accountable, a fixed all-inclusive price inside US$40,000, and a scope honestly sized to what that budget carries. EY says in the proposal what eight case studies and five checks cost in days, and does not promise research volume the fee cannot fund. Michael Harris, Partner, EY Business Consulting South Africa, is personally accountable and is CI's single point of contact.
killRisks: Technical compliance is a gate, not a score. CI states that only the financial proposals of bidders who qualify technically will be reviewed. A bid that breaches a submission rule never has its 30 financial points read at all, however good the price. Every compliance item below therefore outranks every point of persuasion in the document.

The Signed Offeror Representation of Transparency, Integrity, Social Responsibility is a named completeness requirement and the template is NOT in the inputs EY holds. Without it the proposal is incomplete regardless of technical quality. CI must be asked for the form in week 1 of bid preparation, and EY must confirm which legal entity contracts and who has authority to sign it.

Fabricating credentials, client references, CVs, rate-card figures or entity details. Fifty of the 70 technical points (1.2 = 20, 2.2 = 15, 3.1 = 15) rest entirely on inputs that are not in the file, which makes this the strongest temptation in the whole bid and the one failure that would end the client relationship rather than just the bid. Every such gap must carry a [[TO CONFIRM]] placeholder naming exactly what is needed and who supplies it.

Using the SA banking payments POV deck as a sample of work. It is marked 'Draft — not for distribution', it is financial services rather than tourism, conservation or destination branding, and attaching it would be both a breach of a distribution restriction and a near-zero-relevance submission under criterion 2.2. It is not a credential for this bid and should not appear in any annex.

Breaching the 5-page cap on the disciplined reading. Take the cap as applying to the whole technical proposal body — Parts 1, 2 and 3 — with everything else in annexes, because that reading cannot lose points whereas the loose reading can. An evaluator applying the strict reading to a 9-page body may stop reading at page 5, which would most likely cost the staffing and references sections, worth 15 points plus a completeness judgement.

Any price, rate or total appearing in the technical PDF. The technical file is evaluated first and separately; cost leakage into it is a standard disqualification trigger and carries no upside. Effort is expressed in days in the technical proposal and in dollars only in the cost proposal.
Failure to submit two genuinely separate PDFs. The RFP states this twice, which is usually a sign it has caught bidders out before.
Inception payment above 10% of the total. An explicit, checkable breach with no defence.

A budget that cannot be made to fit US$40,000 all-inclusive of profit, fees and taxes at approved EY rates. If EY SA standard rates cannot deliver 12 weeks and four deliverables inside the ceiling, the bid is either loss-making, or the day count is implausibly thin and scores badly on 'reality to market value'. This is a partner decision that must be taken before writing begins, not after.

Scope inflation that the fee cannot fund. EY's own research concludes that eight case studies and five light-touch checks is the most US$40,000 over 12 weeks desk-based can carry. Promising more in the methodology creates a plan the financial evaluator can see is unfunded, and damages 2.1 and the financial score together.
Three client references that are not contactable or not consented. The requirement is explicit and checkable; a reference who declines when called is worse than a weaker reference who answers.

The RFP text in hand ends mid-sentence in the 'Level of Effort and Cost of Services' section, after the US$40,000 ceiling and 'largely desk-based with virtual'. Unknown requirements may sit in the missing text — a level-of-effort ceiling, a required staff mix, a rate constraint. Either obtain the complete RFP from CI or state the assumption explicitly in the cost proposal; do not guess.

Independence and conflict of interest. CI works alongside African Parks, WCS, the Rob Walton Foundation and 21 African governments in the Keystone partnership, and African Parks appears in EY's own benchmark long-list as a potential delivery partner. Any EY audit or advisory relationship with a Keystone partner needs clearing before submission, and the benchmark scan's characterisation of those organisations should be checked for anything a partner could object to.
pageBudget: Page 1, top (approx. 90 words) — Title block and compliance strip. Offeror legal entity, RFP number and title, date, engagement partner and single point of contact (Michael Harris, Partner, EY Business Consulting South Africa), and a four-line compliance strip confirming: separate technical and cost PDFs; body 5 pages excluding annexes; annexes A-F listed; no cost information in this file. This costs almost nothing and tells the evaluator on first glance that the bid is responsive.

Page 1, remainder (approx. 430 words) — 'Our understanding of the assignment and expected outcomes' (criterion 1.1, 5 pts). Three short paragraphs plus one boxed panel. Para 1: the problem as CI frames it and the boundary — the delivery vehicle, not the brands themselves. Para 2: the spectrum from technical-assistance retainer to commercial platform, and the scale test (built for 15, must stretch toward 162 inside a US$1.2bn-a-year partnership). Para 3: the nine mandatory elaboration headings and the seven design aims adopted as the working template, and CI's fill-gaps-not-duplicate test accepted as the standard EY will be judged against. Boxed panel 'What we already know' (approx. 110 words of the 430): the 31-benchmark scan across seven archetypes, Africa's Eden and Boundless Southern Africa already profiled, 13 benchmarks already triaged for deep-dive, cross-referenced to Annex C.

Page 2 (approx. 600 words) — 'Methodology and work plan' (criterion 2.1, 5 pts). A compressed 12-week bar chart occupying roughly a third of the page, showing Activities One to Three against the four deliverables at weeks 2, 5, 10 and 12, with CI review windows marked. Around it: the nine-heading template applied identically to every model; the design-aims matrix named as the pre-agreed frame for recommending the preferred model; the deep-dive programme sized at eight case studies and five light-touch checks with the named interview list; the week 10 stakeholder presentation and the weeks 10-12 adaptation loop, acknowledging that presentations may be needed to several stakeholder groups; and a four-line risk block naming the real evidence gaps (unpublished member fees from commercial collectives, unpublished outcome data from Boundless and KAZA) with mitigations. Effort in days, never dollars. Annex E holds the detailed week-by-week plan and RACI.

Page 3 (approx. 600 words) — 'Relevant experience and recent services' (criteria 1.2 = 20 pts and 2.2 = 15 pts; 35 points, the highest-value page in the document). Upper table: six to eight engagements spanning 5-10 years, columns for client, country, dates, delivering EY entity, EY role, magnitude, and ticks against CI's eight named skill areas, with a coverage line confirming all eight are evidenced. Lower table: three to five engagements completed 2023-2026, each paired with a named sample of work, what it is, what it achieved, and the Annex B page holding it. Roughly 120 words of connecting prose; the rest is table. Both tables must be scoreable without opening an annex. Today this page is almost entirely [[TO CONFIRM]] placeholders and it is the critical path for the bid.

Page 4 (approx. 580 words) — 'Geographical reach and familiarity' (criterion 2.4 = 10 pts, approx. 260 words) and 'Key personnel and staffing' (criterion 3.1 = 15 pts, approx. 320 words). Upper block in two columns: Reach (EY offices and delivery presence across Southern, Eastern and Western Africa, working languages including Portuguese and French, prior country delivery) and Familiarity (evidenced landscape knowledge — SADC TFCAs, KAZA and the UniVisa, NACSO and the Namibian conservancy data spine, MMWCA lease economics, SANParks Wild Card, Fair Trade Tourism mutual recognition), with a line on how the model sits with national tourism boards. Lower block: staffing table with name, role, qualification, years, skill area covered, languages and days allocated, headed by Michael Harris with a stated personal commitment; three lines on management and CI's single point of contact. Day totals must reconcile exactly with page 2 and with the cost proposal. CVs in Annex A.

Page 5 (approx. 450 words) — 'Client references, delivery assurance and assumptions'. Three client references in a compact table (organisation, contact name, role, email, telephone, engagement and year) with confirmation that each has consented to be contacted. A short delivery-assurance block: partner accountability, quality review, independence and conflict position, data handling and confidentiality, and the acceptance route for each of the four deliverables. A clarifications and assumptions list, including that the complete 'Level of Effort and Cost of Services' text was not available and any stated assumption will be reconciled on award, and that CI's list of 15 priority areas is requested at inception. Close with a one-line pointer to the separate Cost Proposal PDF, carrying no figures.

Annexes (not counted against the 5 pages, and where all evidence lives) — A: one-page CVs in a single common format. B: engagement dossier with scope and magnitude, plus the cleared samples of work. C: the 31-benchmark scan, labelled explicitly as an EY bid-stage working paper prepared for this opportunity, not as a client deliverable. D: the signed Offeror Representation of Transparency, Integrity, Social Responsibility once CI supplies the template. E: detailed week-by-week work plan, RACI and interview schedule. F: assumptions, clarification requests and the open-items log. Annexes verify; they never carry a score on their own, so nothing that earns points may exist only in an annex.

Exclusion rule applied across all five pages — no price, day rate, fee total or currency figure anywhere in the technical PDF; effort is expressed only in days. No logos-and-map firm boilerplate. No restatement of the RFP background. Every sentence must be traceable to a scoring criterion, and any sentence that is not should be cut to buy space for page 3.
